blocks.text: A hum crawls across the Kilnyard Drum. Low, steady, with a faint glow on its front like a coal somebody's just blown on.
That's Dov's lead-in. I've got the pitch through my soles before the glow is halfway to me.
"Three. Two. Draw."
Marten and I draw. The note goes into the stone between us and doesn't come out anywhere. No ring. Nothing.
Quist, barefoot on the stand beside the broken one, opens his eyes.
"Again," he says.
So we show him again.
It's still the night of Round 6. The gallery's empty, the bloom's still hanging, thinning by the minute, and the old man who swore off Drums is giving orders on one.
He's put the rest of the side on the stair. All but Dov, who's on the bottom step, because Quist pointed at him and said, "You. Throw. Feet off my floor."
"It's my floor," Dov said. "I live here. Practically."
Quist didn't look at his mouth, so he didn't hear it.

He wanted Marten, not Dov, as my partner. He didn't say why. He pointed at Marten, then at me, then at the flank pair, and Marten took off his boots and walked out to his stand like a man going out to fetch the coal in.
Now Quist says it again. "Again."

Dov throws again. I count again, facing Marten, mouth big so he can read it. We draw on "Draw". Nothing. The floor under my right foot does something small, a shiver, a settling, and I don't wait for it. I look at Quist instead.
His eyes are open already. He's looking at the floor between us.
"Again."

Fourth time, the lead-in comes in and something's off. Not the pitch. The pitch is the same, Dov's a good Caller when he isn't performing. It's the front. It reaches me early. A hair early, the way a cart's earlier than you think on a dry road.
Bloom's thinning. Thin bloom, fast pace. Fast pace, longer wave. Our pair's spaced for the wave we had ten minutes ago.
I open my mouth to count and Quist's hand goes up, flat, like a man stopping a horse.
I shut my mouth. Marten sees me shut it and doesn't draw.
The note goes through us both. It shoves me back on my heels and loses a weight on me and another on Marten and rings the plate behind us like a dropped pan.
Quist steps off his stand.
"What was that, lad."
"Pace went," I say. "The pair was long."
"How long."
"Not much."
"Not much." He nods. "Not much is a doubling. Doubling's ring. Ring's Marks." He holds up one finger, thick as a mallet handle. "One rule. Never draw a pair you can't feel true."
"And if it's nearly true?"
"Then it's not." He looks at Marten. Then at me. "Marks don't come off."

Marten hasn't said a word all this time. He's been watching Quist's mouth the way he watches the Warden's. Now he rubs the back of his neck and nods, slow, the way he nods when one of his girls has told him something he already knew.
"That's fair," he says. "That's a fair rule."
"Agreed," I say. And I mean it. I've got five Marks and a thin whine in my good ear that wasn't there this morning, and I'm not spending a sixth on nearly.
Quist sits on the bottom step next to Dov and puts his boots on.
"Notes go straight," he says, lacing. "Floor tells you what. Eyes tell you where."
Notes go straight.
At the Old Mint, they don't.

The Old Mint Drum is a copy, built into the counting-cellar of a mint that stopped minting before my master was born. Slowstone walls, dressed smooth as a new crown. Somebody spent real money on them. I tap-test them before the match like I promised myself I would: dry, cold, even. Pace five, the Warden says, and pace five it stays. That's not the problem.
The problem is a woman on Old Mint's left-hand stand with a long neck and a longer reach, and Sef has her before the first Half's begun.
"Corners," he says. "Three things about Corners. One, high voice, clean pitch, you'll love her. Two, she raises facing you. Three, no, four, three's important, three is she doesn't voice facing you."
"Where does she voice?"
"Wall."

Their other Caller is a broad man Sef's calling the Ingot, because he's heavy and he's dull and he's worth a lot. The Ingot throws low. Six paces, Oduya says, maybe more. Nobody nulls a six-pace note. Sef doesn't want us Quelling them either. "We're on ten. Hounds next week. I need both of you whole for the Hounds." So the Ingot's notes get body-blocks and Oduya's peg, and the Ingot gets one Peal in the first Half for his trouble, straight through both of us, two weights lighter and still enough.
That leaves Corners.

First throw, she raises. The lead-in comes through the floor sweet as a struck chisel. I've got the pitch, I've got the pair, I've got Marten's eyes. Our two stands are a pace and a bit apart along the straight line from her mouth to our plate. I set my feet. Heels, balls.
She voices.
And at the voicing, not before, she turns.

The beam goes at the wall, not at us. Shallow angle. The glow of the front kisses the slowstone with a soft scrape, like a trowel drawn once across a dry bed, and swings away at a new angle, weight intact, and comes for us from the side.
Notes don't turn corners. Everybody knows that.
The floor told me what that note was, down to a quarter-tone. It never told me where it was going.

Now it's coming across our pair instead of down it. Across a bank, the path to Marten and the path to me aren't the same two lengths any more. I don't know what they are. I can't feel it. That's the whole point. I can't feel it.
I shut my mouth.

Marten reads the shut mouth. He doesn't draw. I don't draw. The note goes through me first, then him, and it's lighter by two when it hits our Last Plate. Still enough. Still on pitch. Oduya walked the peg last Breath, but the peg's on the rail for anyone to read, and Corners reads it.
Three counts. Peal.
The Old Mint gallery's a stone one, low and close, and the roar comes down through the whine in my right ear like rain through a split slate.
"Interesting," says Sef. And then nothing, for a while.
We don't lose because Corners is good. We lose because she's good every throw.

Every throw, she raises facing us. Every throw, I get the pitch and set the pair, because the one time I don't, she'll throw it straight and Peal it straight down the middle. Every throw, I stand there with my mouth ready to say "Draw", watching the front.
And every throw, she turns.

Sometimes the bank sends the front wide and it rattles a side plate and scores nothing. Sometimes our blocks knock enough weight off it, and Oduya's peg is just far enough away, and it hits the Last Plate a semitone and a hair off and rattles like a lid. Oduya says nothing when that happens. She just walks the peg again at the next Breath with her mouth very small.
Dov, meanwhile, is having the night of his life.

Old Mint's Dampers stand square and draw straight and he walks round them. He gets the Lamplighter in early. Late in the first Half he puts one high past their right-hand Damper's ear, dead straight, just mean, and it Peals, and he turns to their Scribe and bows. "That was the Counterfeit. Because this is a mint. You're welcome."
Second Half, he gets the Long Goodnight. Three Peals. The Ingot gets one more through in the same Half, low and slow through both of us, and it's three all.
Then it's the last throw of the match, and it's hers.

I know before she raises. She knows I know. She raises facing me anyway, and the lead-in comes down through the floor and the pitch is lovely, and I've got a pair for it. The flank pair. The best one on this floor. I can feel how true it would be, straight down the line, if she'd only throw straight.
Marten's watching my mouth.
She voices. She turns.
The front scrapes the wall and swings, and for half a count I think, it's a shallow bank. It's nearly straight. It's nearly true.
Nearly.
I shut my mouth.
It goes through us. It takes a weight off each of us and arrives at our plate at weight three, dead on pitch, and the plate rings. One. Two. Three.
Three to four, Old Mint.
The Warden doesn't call a Toll for either of us all night. Nothing to call. Five, Halloway. Thirty-seven, Sallow. Same as we came in.
After, on the bench, everybody's packing round me and I'm drawing on my palm with Oduya's chalk.
A line for the wall. A dot for Corners' stand. Two dots for our pair.

Then I fold it. In my head, the way you'd fold a template to check a pair of mouldings. Fold the Drum along the wall, and Corners lands on the far side of the stone, a mirror Corners standing in the rock. A banked beam is just a straight beam from her mirror. And from her mirror, the straight line to Marten and the straight line to me are two different lengths from what they were from her real stand.
So across a bank, the gap between two stands isn't what matters. The path is.
Space for the path, not the gap.
I sit and look at my palm. It's a good answer. It's three hours late.
"Wren Halloway," says Oduya, very quietly, and puts her hand over my chalk hand and closes it. "Boots."
That night, the Kilnyard Drum.
Quist's already down there when we come in. Not on the stair. On the floor, boots off and paired on the bottom step, sitting on the stand next to our rocking Last Stand with one hand flat on it.
He holds his other hand out to me. I open my palm. He reads the chalk, and the smudges, and says, "Good. Late. Good."
Then he looks up at all five of us. Sef, Dov, Oduya, Marten, me. He takes his time over each face. He's reading us, I realise. Making sure we can all see his mouth.
"Cup final," he says. "Thirty-one years back. Bad night. My own fault."
Nobody says anything.
"Not true," Quist says. "Any of it."
Oduya lets out a breath I think she's been holding since drill night, weeks ago.
"There was no final," she says.

"No. There wasn't." He doesn't hear her. He doesn't need to; he's watching her mouth, and he nods to it. "There was a partner. Linus Abbot. Best Damper I ever stood beside. We found what the lad found." His chin goes at me. "Half a wave. One instant. Not two. We did it in the Cathedral Drum. Training night. Nobody watching."
His fingers are going on the stand while he talks. That stop-start thing he does on tables at the Lime Barrow. Tap, tap-tap, rest.
"And the floor answered," he says.
My feet are on the stone. I keep them very still.
"Answered what?" says Sef. Then, because Quist didn't catch it, he says it again, slow, facing him. "Answered. What?"

"Don't know." Quist's voice is flat as ever, and too loud, and it doesn't shake. "Answered. Came up through the stand. Like a man knocking on the far side of a wall. We weren't drunk. We weren't ring-touched. We were young. We did the right thing. We told the Chapter."
He stops tapping.

"Two weeks later, training session. Chapter's Drum. Chapter's Callers. We draw. They don't stop. Hard notes, one after another, into us both. Lit and still throwing. Wrote it down as an accident." He touches one ear, then the other. "Paid me a pension. Paid me to say Cup final. I took it."
"Linus?" Marten says. Quietly. Quist reads it anyway.
"Drank himself dead. Nine years after."
Nobody moves. Up on the gallery, a drip comes off the kiln flue and hits the stone.
"Why?" Dov says. His voice has gone very small for Dov. "Why would they do that? For a ghost quell?"
"Don't know," Quist says. "Thirty-one years. Still don't know." He looks at me again. "You do it every match. On this floor."
I don't say what I've felt on this floor. I nearly do. His eyes are on my mouth, waiting, and I find there's nothing in it.
Quist stands up off the stand. Stiff in the knees. He picks up his boots and doesn't put them on.
"Drill night," he says. "All of you. Bare feet." He points at Dov. "You too."
"I'm the Caller."
"You were sick in a bucket and then you counted three clean ones," Quist says. "You're a Damper on drill night."
Dov opens his mouth, shuts it, and doesn't name anything.
The letter comes an hour later.
Jory brings it down the stair. A man in Chapter grey left it with her uncle at the kiln-house door, she says, and wouldn't wait for an answer. Good paper. A red seal pressed with a bell.
Sef takes it, turns it over twice, and holds it out to Oduya. "Your eyes are better than mine."
I watch him not look at it. I put that away with the notebook.
Oduya breaks the seal and reads aloud, in her full-names voice.

"'To the Scribe and side of Kilnyard. With the Chapter's compliments, and its congratulations on a fine Run. Round 9 of the Midwinter Run, being the round on which promotion will be decided, will by custom be played not at Kilnyard but at the Chapterhouse Drum, as the Chapter's guests. The Chapter looks forward to watching Kilnyard on its floor.'"
She lowers the letter. She lowers her voice, which is worse.
"By custom," she says.
Quist can't hear any of it. He's watching her mouth. I watch his face go grey round the edges, the colour of old mortar.
An hour ago he told us what the Chapter does to people who play the Dead Air on its floors, and now the Chapter has asked us to come and play on one.
